sentence: Your arm stays smooth in the same bath.
claim: Water-immersion wrinkling occurs in the glabrous (hairless) skin of the fingers, palms and soles, not in hairy skin such as the forearm.
source_title: Haseleu J, Omerbašić D, Frenzel H, Gross M, Lewin GR (2014). Water-induced finger wrinkles do not affect touch acuity or dexterity in handling wet objects. PLOS ONE 9:e84949
note: Excerpt (Haseleu 2014 intro): human non-hairy (glabrous) skin of the fingers, palms and soles wrinkles after prolonged exposure to water.

sentence: It looks like skin soaking up water and swelling, like a sponge.
claim: Water-immersion wrinkling is commonly attributed to skin swelling by osmosis (absorbing water); that explanation is not supported.
source_title: Wilder-Smith EP (2004). Water immersion wrinkling: physiology and use as an indicator of sympathetic function. Clin Auton Res 14:125–131 (abstract)
note: Search excerpts: osmosis, once a common explanation, has been ruled out; wrinkling depends on intact sympathetic innervation (Wilder-Smith 2004 review; Haseleu 2014). 'It looks like' states the appearance, c11 the correction.

sentence: It's the story we grew up with, and it's wrong.
claim: The swelling/osmosis explanation is incorrect: wrinkling requires intact nerve supply (restates c2, c3).
source_title: Wilder-Smith EP (2004). Water immersion wrinkling: physiology and use as an indicator of sympathetic function. Clin Auton Res 14:125–131 (abstract)
note: Restates c2–c3; 'the story we grew up with' is framing (no claim about how many people believe it).

sentence: Almost a century ago, doctors noticed something odd: a finger whose nerve had been cut stayed perfectly smooth in the bath.
claim: In the 1930s Lewis and Pickering observed that skin supplied by a damaged (median) nerve did not wrinkle in water.
source_title: Haseleu J, Omerbašić D, Frenzel H, Gross M, Lewin GR (2014). Water-induced finger wrinkles do not affect touch acuity or dexterity in handling wet objects. PLOS ONE 9:e84949
note: Excerpt: in the 1930s, Lewis and Pickering first described the absence of wrinkling in patients with median nerve palsy. Sources date the paper 1935 or 1936; on screen '1930s'. 'Almost a century ago' (≈90 years) is computed.

sentence: So the wrinkles come from your nerves.
claim: Water-immersion wrinkling is produced by the nervous system: it depends on sympathetic nerve fibres to the fingers.
source_title: Wilder-Smith EP (2004). Water immersion wrinkling: physiology and use as an indicator of sympathetic function. Clin Auton Res 14:125–131 (abstract)
note: Excerpt: if the sympathetic nerve fibers to the fingers are cut, they no longer wrinkle in water; the wrinkling test is used as a bedside test of sympathetic function.

sentence: In water, they narrow the tiny vessels under each fingertip, the pad shrinks a little, and the skin on top buckles.
claim: Immersion causes sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction in the fingertips; the loss of pulp volume makes the overlying skin buckle into wrinkles.
source_title: Wilder-Smith EP (2004). Water immersion wrinkling: physiology and use as an indicator of sympathetic function. Clin Auton Res 14:125–131 (abstract)
note: Excerpt: Wilder-Smith and Chow (2003) showed wrinkling is directly linked to vasoconstriction (digital blood flow drops as the skin puckers). How water triggers the reflex (sweat ducts, electrolytes) is still studied: badge.

sentence: A wrinkle is a reflex, one doctors use to test a nerve.
claim: Because it depends on intact sympathetic nerves, immersion (or EMLA-induced) wrinkling is used clinically as a bedside test of sympathetic nerve function.
source_title: Wilder-Smith EP (2004). Water immersion wrinkling: physiology and use as an indicator of sympathetic function. Clin Auton Res 14:125–131 (abstract)
note: Excerpt: these discoveries led to the implementation of the wrinkling test as a bedside test of sympathetic nerve function. A neurologist confirms the wording.

sentence: Why we have it is argued: one study found a wet grip, the next found none.
claim: A 2013 study found wrinkled fingers moved submerged objects faster than unwrinkled ones (no effect for dry objects).
source_title: Kareklas K, Nettle D, Smulders TV (2013). Water-induced finger wrinkles improve handling of wet objects. Biology Letters 9:20120999
note: Excerpt: participants manipulated submerged objects more quickly with wrinkled fingers; secondary reports give about 12% faster with ~20 volunteers (not voiced).

sentence: Why we have it is argued: one study found a wet grip, the next found none.
claim: A 2014 study of 40 people found wrinkling did not improve dexterity with wet objects or touch acuity; the purpose of wrinkling remains debated.
source_title: Haseleu J, Omerbašić D, Frenzel H, Gross M, Lewin GR (2014). Water-induced finger wrinkles do not affect touch acuity or dexterity in handling wet objects. PLOS ONE 9:e84949
note: Excerpt: skin wrinkling did not improve dexterity in handling wet objects; the wet-object advantage could not be reproduced. Badge 'debated'.

sentence: It only happens on the hairless skin of hands and feet, where the dead layer runs thickest, nearly two sheets of paper.
claim: Immersion wrinkling occurs on the glabrous skin of the hands and feet (restates c0).
source_title: Haseleu J, Omerbašić D, Frenzel H, Gross M, Lewin GR (2014). Water-induced finger wrinkles do not affect touch acuity or dexterity in handling wet objects. PLOS ONE 9:e84949

sentence: It only happens on the hairless skin of hands and feet, where the dead layer runs thickest, nearly two sheets of paper.
claim: The palm's stratum corneum measured about 173 µm (vs 16.8 µm on the cheek), about 1.7 times a 100 µm sheet of copy paper.
source_title: Egawa M, Hirao T, Takahashi M (2007). In vivo estimation of stratum corneum thickness … Acta Derm Venereol 87:4–8
note: Excerpt: palm 173.0 µm, cheek 16.8 µm (confocal Raman, 15 adults). 'Nearly two sheets of paper' computed (173/100 = 1.73). Thickest of the sites measured there (palm vs cheek, forearm, back of hand); soles are thicker still in other studies, not voiced.

sentence: So your fingers don't wrinkle because they're soaked.
claim: Finger wrinkling is not caused by the skin soaking up water (restates c1, c11).
source_title: Wilder-Smith EP (2004). Water immersion wrinkling: physiology and use as an indicator of sympathetic function. Clin Auton Res 14:125–131 (abstract)

sentence: They wrinkle because your nerves decide to.
claim: Wrinkling is produced by a sympathetic nerve reflex (restates c3, c4); 'decide' is a figure of speech for an automatic reflex.
source_title: Wilder-Smith EP (2004). Water immersion wrinkling: physiology and use as an indicator of sympathetic function. Clin Auton Res 14:125–131 (abstract)
note: Restates c3–c4. Dermatologist/neurologist checks 'decide' reads as figurative (it is involuntary).
